subject: Physics
scope: 14 original AQA AS Waves recall flashcards, closing selected gaps after reviewing existing cards, not a full specification sign-off.
notes: Written-paper concepts only. Covers first-harmonic formula and dependences, RP1 graph interpretation, harmonics/snapshots, sound reflections, coherence, white-light interference/gratings, general critical-angle relation, air index and path/phase. Retain original card IDs, saved progress and exact first-mock scope.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a stretched string fixed at both ends, state the first-harmonic frequency formula using length L, tension T and mass per unit length μ.
accept: f1 = (1/2L) sqrt(T/mu)
One over twice the length times the square root of tension divided by mass per length.
reject: f = 2L sqrt(T/mu)
f1 = (1/(2L)) sqrt(mu/T)

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At fixed tension and mass per unit length, what happens to a string's first-harmonic frequency if the vibrating length doubles?
accept: It halves.
The frequency becomes half its original value.
The first harmonic decreases by a factor of two.
reject: The frequency doubles.
It stays unchanged.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: At fixed length and tension, how does the first-harmonic frequency change if the mass per unit length of a string quadruples?
accept: It halves.
Frequency falls to one half.
It is divided by two because frequency is inversely proportional to the square root of mass per unit length.
reject: It quadruples.
It doubles.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a fixed vibrating length L and mass per unit length μ, what is the gradient of a graph of first-harmonic frequency squared against tension?
accept: The slope is 1 divided by 4 L squared mu.
Gradient equals 1/(4 times length squared times mass per unit length).
reject: 4L²μ.
The gradient is 1/(2L).

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a string fixed at both ends in the second harmonic, how many nodes and antinodes are there, counting end nodes?
accept: Three nodes and two antinodes.
3 nodes and 2 antinodes.
Two loops with a node at each end and a node in the middle.
reject: Two nodes and three antinodes.
Three antinodes and four nodes.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: A stationary string wave is at its maximum upward displacement. What will its pattern look like half a period later?
cards.back: The antinodes have equal maximum displacement in the opposite direction, while the nodes stay fixed.
accept: The antinodes have equal maximum displacement in the opposite direction, while the nodes stay fixed.
The displaced loops invert after half a cycle; nodes remain stationary.
Opposite maximum displacement at antinodes with all nodes unmoved.
reject: The whole pattern has moved half a wavelength along the string.
Every node moves to an antinode.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: How can stationary sound waves form when sound is reflected?
cards.back: Incident and reflected waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose.
accept: Incident and reflected waves of the same frequency travel in opposite directions and superpose.
The original sound and its reflection superpose while travelling in opposite directions.
Oppositely travelling waves of the same frequency interfere to make a stationary pattern.
reject: The sound must change frequency on reflection.
Only one travelling wave is needed.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why does illuminating two slits with one wavefront help produce a stable interference pattern?
cards.back: The two slits act as coherent sources because their waves maintain a constant phase difference.
accept: The two slits act as coherent sources because their waves maintain a constant phase difference.
Both slits receive the same incoming wave and produce coherent waves.
Splitting a single wavefront ensures a fixed relative phase for the two sources.
reject: The two slits produce light with random relative phase.
The slit separation always equals one wavelength.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Why do white-light double-slit fringes from different colours overlap more away from the central white fringe?
cards.back: Different wavelengths have different fringe spacings, so their bright fringes occur at different positions and eventually overlap.
accept: Different wavelengths have different fringe spacings, so their bright fringes occur at different positions and eventually overlap.
The colours have different wavelengths and fringe spacings causing coloured fringes to overlap.
Different wavelength patterns become superposed beyond the central fringe.
reject: All wavelengths have identical fringe spacings.
The frequency of each colour changes along the screen.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For white light incident normally on a diffraction grating, what is seen in the zero-order maximum?
cards.back: A white maximum because the colours are not angularly separated at zero order.
accept: A white maximum because the colours are not angularly separated at zero order.
Zero order is white.
The central grating maximum is white, with all wavelengths at zero diffraction angle.
reject: A red central maximum.
The zero-order maximum is a full spectrum.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For a ray going from refractive index n₁ to lower index n₂, state the general critical-angle equation.
cards.back: sin θc = n₂/n₁, where n₁ > n₂.
accept: sin θc = n₂/n₁, where n₁ > n₂.
Sine of the critical angle equals lower refractive index divided by higher refractive index.
sin critical angle = n2/n1 for n1 greater than n2.
reject: sin θc = n₁/n₂ where n₁ > n₂.
The critical angle is always 90 degrees.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Approximately what refractive index should you use for air in AQA AS Physics calculations?
accept: 1.00 (approximately one).
About one.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: Two initially in-phase waves have path difference Δx and wavelength λ. What phase difference in radians does this path difference produce?
accept: Δφ = 2πΔx/λ.
Phase difference equals 2 pi times path difference divided by wavelength.
2π times delta x over lambda.
reject: Δφ = 2πλ/Δx.
The phase difference is always zero.

cards.subject: Physics
cards.front: For normally incident white light on a diffraction grating, why does the red first-order maximum appear at a larger angle than the violet?
cards.back: Red light has a longer wavelength, so d sin θ = mλ gives a greater angle at the same order.
accept: Red light has a longer wavelength, so d sin θ = mλ gives a greater angle at the same order.
Red has a larger wavelength so diffracts through a bigger angle.
From d sin theta = m lambda, longer red wavelength means larger theta.
reject: Red has a smaller wavelength than violet.
All colours in the first order have the same angle.
